loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM.
question:
A risk committee member at a US public pension plan asks staff for statements that correctly contrast the CAPM with multifactor models. Staff propose four:

I. In the CAPM the market diversifies away idiosyncratic risk; in multifactor models the tradeable version of a factor does so.

II. In the CAPM the average investor holds the market; in multifactor models the average investor holds an equal exposure to every factor.

III. In the CAPM an asset’s risk is measured by its CAPM beta; in multifactor models it is measured by its factor betas.

IV. In the CAPM assets paying off when the market return is low have low risk premiums; in multifactor models assets paying off in the bad times defined by the factors have low risk premiums.

Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: II and IV only
options.C: I, II and III only
options.D: I, III and IV only

solution:
Committee member asks which four staff statements correctly contrast the CAPM with multifactor models.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s “Multifactor Model Lessons” table sets the CAPM and multifactor models side by side. “The key lessons in the multifactor world are in fact the same from the CAPM”; what changes is the mechanism or the definition of bad times.

| Lesson | CAPM (market factor) | Multifactor models |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The market diversifies away idiosyncratic risk | The tradeable version of a factor diversifies away idiosyncratic risk |
| 2 | Own optimal exposure of the market portfolio | Own optimal exposure of each factor risk |
| 3 | Average investor holds the market | Average investor holds the market |

question: A board member of a Singapore sovereign fund reviews the 2008 returns: equities, corporate and high-yield bonds, real estate, hedge funds and commodities all fell together. She argues that “diversification is dead and factor risk theory has failed.” The CRO is asked to reply. Which reply is most consistent with the multifactor view of the crisis?

options.A: She is right: losses common to so many asset classes are a rejection of multifactor models, so the fund should rely on asset-class labels and hold mainly cash and safe-haven bonds.
options.B: The common losses are consistent with a multifactor model in which many asset classes share exposures to the same factors; asset-class labels hid those exposures, but diversification itself is not dead.
options.C: The losses show that the CAPM was complete: the market was the only factor at work, and every asset class fell because each had a high beta to the market portfolio.
options.D: Diversification would have worked had correlations been estimated with more data, because correlations between asset classes are constant over time, including during bad times.

solution:
Board member says 2008 proved diversification dead; CRO replies from the multifactor view.

GARP opens and closes the chapter with the 2008 and 2009 crisis. In 2008 most risky assets fell together: large-cap US equities −37%, international and emerging equities more, corporate, emerging-market and high-yield bonds, real estate, private capital, hedge funds (about −20%) and commodities (over −30%). Only cash and safe-haven sovereign bonds rose.

Section 1.8 explains this through the multifactor lens: the simultaneous poor performance “is consistent with an underlying multifactor model in which many asset classes were exposed to the same factors”. A portfolio manager at a French insurer compares two EUR stocks using the CAPM and a two-factor model (market factor and an economic-growth factor whose bad times are periods of low growth). The growth factor has a positive risk premium.

|---|---|---|
| CAPM beta | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| Two-factor model: beta to the market factor | 1.00 | 1.00 |

| Return volatility (%) | 30.00 | 18.00 |
| Dividend yield (%) | 1.50 | 3.20 |

Two stocks with equal CAPM beta but different growth-factor betas; volatility and dividend yield given.

The direction comes from the bad-times logic. If the growth factor’s bad times are periods of low growth, a positive growth beta means the stock does badly when growth is low: it loses in a bad time, so it is risky and must offer a higher premium. loText: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk.
question:
A senior risk analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is briefing the investment committee on whether a larger allocation to government bonds would protect the fund’s AUD 4.2 billion equity sleeve against volatility shocks. She shows the following monthly correlations (March 1986 to December 2011), together with the fund’s current bond duration of 6.8 years.

|  | VIX changes | Stock returns | Bond returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| VIX changes | 1.00 | −0.39 | 0.12 |
| Stock returns | −0.39 | 1.00 | −0.01 |
| Bond returns | 0.12 | −0.01 | 1.00 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.A: Because bond returns are positively correlated with VIX changes, a larger bond allocation would pay off reliably in nearly every high-volatility episode.
options.B: The relevant figure is the stock-bond correlation of −0.01, which shows that bonds neither help nor hurt the fund when volatility rises.
options.C: Bonds offer some but not much respite: they tend to fare better than stocks when the VIX rises, but they do not always pay off in highly volatile periods.
options.D: The positive correlation of 0.12 means that bond prices tend to fall when volatility rises, so bonds add to the fund’s volatility exposure.

solution:
Superannuation fund analyst asks whether more bonds would protect the equity sleeve, given the correlation matrix of VIX changes, stock returns and bond returns.

**Concept and theory**

Volatility is one of the three most important macro factors in GARP’s account, and it is a bad-times factor: when volatility rises, stocks tend to fall. GARP measures volatility risk with the VIX, the option-implied volatility of the S&P 500. The first and most obvious way to reduce exposure to volatility shocks is to hold assets that are less hurt by them. Bonds are the natural candidate, and GARP tests this directly with a correlation table of monthly VIX changes, stock returns and bond returns from March 1986 to December 2011.

options.A: In 2008 and 2009 volatility caused many risky assets to fall together while risk-free bonds did very well, but in the turbulence of the late 1970s and early 1980s bonds did terribly, as did equities.

UK insurer’s auditor checks the historical episodes cited in a board paper that relies on gilts as the main volatility defense.

question: A risk consultant at a Singapore bank is writing a report for a client that plans to hedge its SGD-funded global equity portfolio with instruments linked to the VIX. The client asks what such a hedge would actually be exposed to. Which of the following statements should the consultant include in the report?

options.A: The VIX is a pure measure of smooth, diffusive equity volatility, so a VIX-linked hedge carries no exposure to jump risk or skewness risk.
options.B: The VIX is computed from realized S&P 500 return volatility, so a VIX-linked hedge carries no exposure to the volatility risk premium.
options.C: Research finds uncertainty risk to be unrelated to volatility risk, so a VIX-linked hedge leaves the client’s uncertainty exposure untouched.
options.D: The VIX bundles volatility with jump and skewness risk and the volatility risk premium, and it also captures uncertainty, which is distinct from but highly correlated with volatility.

solution:
Singapore consultant explains what a VIX-linked hedge is actually exposed to.

**Concept and theory**

A second challenge in managing volatility risk is measurement: the VIX is not a clean, single-risk gauge. GARP’s footnote 6 says the VIX is built from option volatilities on the S&P 500 by the CBOE and “captures a variety of risks related to higher movements, including volatility itself, but also jump risk and skewness risk,” while its main components are “volatility and the volatility risk premium.” Because the VIX is option-implied (risk-neutral), it contains the premium investors pay for protection, not only the volatility that will be realized.

Japanese equity fund, which must stay fully invested, wants a position that pays off when volatility spikes.

The second mitigation method is to buy volatility protection in derivatives markets. question: A treasury analyst at a French bank is presenting the economics of volatility to newly hired analysts on the derivatives desk. Which of the following statements about the volatility premium is most accurate?

options.A: Volatility is a factor with a positive price of risk, so a long volatility position, like a long equity position, earns a positive expected return over time.
options.B: A negative price of volatility risk is a feature of the aggregate equity market only; fixed income, currency and commodity markets carry a positive price.
options.C: Investors on average pay to avoid volatility risk: VIX implied volatility exceeds realized volatility by about 2% to 3%, so the premium is collected by selling protection.
options.D: The volatility premium is earned by buying out-of-the-money put options, because on average such options are cheap relative to the volatility subsequently realized.

solution:
French bank’s treasury analyst explains the volatility premium to new derivatives analysts.

**Concept and theory**

Most factors have a positive premium: we go long equities and the long position earns a positive expected return over time. Volatility is different. GARP: “Volatility is a factor with a negative price of risk.” Investors are “so concerned about volatility, on average, that they are willing to pay to avoid volatility risk, rather than be paid to take it on.” The evidence is in option prices: “VIX implied volatilities are approximately 2% to 3%, on average, higher than realized volatilities.” Options are therefore expensive on average, and “to collect a volatility premium requires selling volatility protection, especially selling out-of-the-money put options.”

question: A member of the risk committee of a Chinese insurer’s asset management arm is reviewing four CNY client mandates that propose selling volatility protection through index put options. Which client is most suitable to be a seller of volatility protection?

options.A: A long-horizon, unleveraged endowment with no large payouts due in market stress, which can sit through very large losses when volatility spikes and risky assets fall together.
options.B: A leveraged fund that must meet margin calls and investor redemptions during market stress, but which values the high and steady premiums earned in calm periods.
options.C: A pension plan that reasons that, because the price of volatility risk is negative, selling put protection is a way to reduce the risk of its existing equity holdings.

Chinese insurer’s risk committee decides which client is suited to selling volatility protection.

GARP compares selling volatility to selling insurance: “During normal times, you collect a premium for withstanding the inevitable large losses that occur every decade or so. GARP: “Rebalancing as a portfolio strategy is actually a short volatility strategy.” A rebalancer sells assets that have risen and buys those that have fallen. loText: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama- French model as an example.
question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore sovereign wealth fund is presenting to newly hired analysts. She explains why the fund’s investment committee implements its factor exposures through dynamic factors such as size and value rather than by targeting macro factors such as inflation and economic growth directly. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Dynamic factors are attractive mainly because they are unrelated to macro risk, so they give the fund return streams that are independent of the fundamental risks of the economy.
options.B: Economic growth is the one macro factor that is traded in scale, so growth exposure can be implemented directly, while inflation exposure has to be obtained through dynamic factors.
options.C: Macro factors such as inflation and growth are usually not directly traded in scale, volatility being the exception, whereas dynamic factors can be easily implemented and still reflect macro risk.
options.D: Because they are tradeable, dynamic factors fully replace macro factors, so a fund holding size and value factor portfolios no longer carries any exposure to inflation or growth shocks.

solution:
A sovereign wealth fund analyst explains why factor exposures are implemented through dynamic factors rather than macro factors.

Factor theory says that assets earn risk premiums because they are exposed to factors that do badly in bad times. GARP Chapter 2 sorts factors into two families. Macro, fundamental-based factors are economy-wide variables: economic growth, inflation, volatility, productivity and demographic risk. Investment, or style, factors are tradeable investment strategies: the market portfolio, value-growth, momentum and so on.

question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese asset manager is preparing a short report on the Fama-French (1993) model for the firm’s equity desk. She drafts four statements and must decide which to include.

I. SMB is the return on a portfolio of small stocks minus the return on a portfolio of big stocks, where small and big refer simply to market capitalization.

question: A risk analyst at a Hong Kong family office is drafting a briefing on the risk profile of US equity momentum strategies, using the evidence for January 1965 to December 2011 and the record of the largest momentum crashes. Which of the following statements in the draft is NOT correct?

options.A: Of the eleven largest momentum crashes, seven occurred during the 2008 financial crisis, three during the Great Depression of the 1930s and one in 2001.
options.B: Momentum strategies are negatively skewed: over January 1965 to December 2011 the skewness of the WML strategy was about −1.43.
options.C: Momentum profits appear to vary over the business cycle, to depend on the state of the stock market and to be linked to liquidity.
options.D: The largest momentum drawdowns have been concentrated in periods of high volatility in which policymakers interrupted the natural progression of asset prices.

solution:
Briefing on momentum risk: which statement about crashes, skew, macro links and policy periods is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP characterizes momentum risk on four dimensions.

| Dimension | GARP evidence |
|---|---|
| Crash record | Eleven largest crashes: seven in the Great Depression (1930s), one in 2001, three in the 2008 financial crisis |
| Distribution | Negatively skewed; skewness of WML in Figure 2.6 is −1.43 |
| Macro links | Profits vary over the business cycle, depend on the state of the stock market, and are linked to liquidity |
| Policy and volatility | Drawdowns concentrated when policymakers interrupted natural progressions of momentum; these were also times of high volatility |

loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.
question: The CRO of a US university endowment is comparing the rational (risk-based) explanations of the value and momentum premiums before approving USD 300 million of factor tilts. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Both rational stories are equally developed: just as value firms carry high and asymmetric adjustment costs, momentum firms are risky because their capital cannot be redeployed in bad times.
options.B: In the rational story, value risk can largely be diversified away across many value stocks, so the value premium compensates mainly for firm-specific losses that happen to coincide with recessions.
options.C: Value stocks move together, much of their risk cannot be diversified away and their betas rise in bad times such as low investment growth, whereas the rational story of momentum is still far from fully fleshed out.
options.D: Rational stories hold that value’s bad times always coincide with bad times for the economy, so the late-1990s boom, when value lost heavily, is inconsistent with any risk-based value premium.

solution:
Endowment CRO compares the rational explanations of the value and momentum premiums.

**Concept and theory**

In the rational (pricing kernel) view, a risk premium exists because it compensates for losing money during bad times; the key is defining those bad times.

Value. Value stocks move together with other value stocks after controlling for market exposure (and covary negatively with growth stocks). Some value risk can be diversified in portfolios, but a large amount cannot; under the APT the undiversifiable remainder must be priced, giving a value premium. Value’s bad times do not always line up with the economy’s: value did badly in the late 1970s and early 1980s, the early-1990s recession and 2008, but also in the late-1990s boom. loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.
question:
A senior analyst at a sovereign wealth fund is building a slide that links four behavioral mechanisms to the factor premium each is used to explain in the reading:

(1) Investors overextrapolate past growth rates into the future and bid glamour stocks up too high.

(2) Investors are loss averse and use mental accounting, so a stock burned by dismal prior performance is viewed as riskier.

(3) Informed investors are overconfident and attribute their successes to their own skill, pushing prices above fundamental values.

(4) News watchers receive signals of firm value with delay, and these are only partially incorporated into prices, while other investors trade only on past prices.

Which mapping is correct?

options.A: Value: (1) and (2); momentum overreaction: (4); momentum underreaction: (3)
options.B: Value: (1) and (2); momentum overreaction: (3); momentum underreaction: (4)
options.C: Value: (2) only; momentum overreaction: (1) and (3); momentum underreaction: (4)
options.D: Value: (1), (2) and (4); momentum overreaction: (3); momentum underreaction: none

solution:
Map four behavioral mechanisms to value, momentum overreaction and momentum underreaction.

**Concept and theory**

Behavioral explanations say a factor premium arises from investor behavior that is not arbitraged away.

Value. (i) Overextrapolation (Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny, 1994): investors overextrapolate past growth rates into the future, so growth (“glamour”) stocks are bid up too high; when the growth does not materialize, their returns are low relative to value stocks. Value stocks are not fundamentally riskier, just cheap.
